stem:
The Earth may be considered as a uniform sphere of radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m.

Cambridge is at a point on the Earth’s surface that has a latitude of 52.2° north of the Equator, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

[[fig:f1]]

As the Earth spins on its axis, Cambridge moves in a circle that is parallel to the Equator but with a smaller radius.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Show that the radius of the circle around which Cambridge moves is 3.90 × 10⁶ m.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the speed at which Cambridge moves around the circle.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.lead: A student of mass 58.6 kg stands on horizontal ground in Cambridge.
parts.text: Determine the magnitude of the resultant force that acts to cause the circular motion of the student.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
On Fig. 1.2, draw an arrow to show the direction of the resultant force that acts on the student.

[[fig:f2]]

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
On Fig. 1.3, draw labelled arrows from the student to show the directions of the forces that act on the student to cause the resultant force in (b)(ii).

[[fig:f3]]

figures.caption: Fig. 1.1
figures.alt: A diagram of the Earth showing the Equator, axis, North and South Poles, and Cambridge at 52.2° north latitude.

figures.caption: Fig. 1.2 (not to scale)
figures.alt: A student stands on the curved surface of the Earth, with a dashed line extending diagonally inward from the student.

figures.caption: Fig. 1.3 (not to scale)
figures.alt: A student stands on a curved Earth surface, with a dashed line extending diagonally inward from the student.
